cim: Why AI Is Redefining Fiduciary Best Practices
cim_eredeti: Why AI Is Redefining Fiduciary Best Practices
szoveg_eredeti:
Don Trone explains how preserving yesterday's practices without examining today's capabilities may itself present fiduciary risk

Twenty-five years ago, fiduciary best practices brought greater structure and accountability to investment stewardship. They provided professionals with a disciplined process for organizing responsibilities, evaluating investments, managing conflicts, and documenting decisions.

Those contributions remain valuable. Yet the emergence of Artificial Intelligence has exposed the limitations of treating those practices as the highest expression of fiduciary excellence.

Augmented Intelligence, informed by the principles of Behavioral Governance, offers a more comprehensive model because it strengthens the human judgment that ultimately determines whether a fiduciary process serves the best interests of others.

This is not an argument against traditional fiduciary practices. It is an argument about adequacy. A framework can remain useful while becoming less capable than a more advanced alternative. The availability of more powerful tools and methods should prompt the profession to reconsider what it teaches, measures, and expects from fiduciaries.

The central limitation is straightforward. A process can be complete while the reasoning behind it remains weak. A committee can review reports, follow its investment policy, and record a unanimous vote while overlooking a flawed assumption. Members may defer to a dominant personality, suppress disagreement, or accept an advisor’s confidence as evidence. The documentation can appear exemplary even when the decision warrants deeper scrutiny.

Artificial Intelligence makes this gap more visible. It can compare documents, organize evidence, generate alternative scenarios, and identify questions that deserve investigation. These capabilities expand what professionals can examine before acting. Yet faster analysis alone does not produce better stewardship. A system that accelerates an unquestioned assumption may simply help a committee arrive at a poor decision more efficiently.

That is why the distinction between Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Intelligence matters. Artificial Intelligence is the technology. Augmented Intelligence is the purpose-driven partnership in which technology enhances human capability, judgment, and execution. Behavioral Governance provides the framework for developing, exercising, and evaluating those capabilities. Together, they connect analytical power with disciplined human responsibility, transforming information into informed action and accountable decision-making.

Behavioral Governance can be understood through the interrelationships between leadership, stewardship, and decision-making. It focuses attention on how people interpret evidence, respond to pressure, manage competing interests, and translate commitments into action. The central question is not simply whether a required task was completed, but whether those responsible, exercised sound judgment in carrying it out.

One way to operationalize this perspective is through a structured framework that examines four interconnected dimensions:

The objective is to connect what professionals know, how they make decisions, and how those decisions are ultimately reflected in observable actions and outcomes.

This approach emphasizes “Signals” – evidence that can be seen, discussed, and evaluated rather than relying solely on credentials, intentions, or documented processes. Examples include a board member requesting contrary evidence before a vote, a committee chair encouraging dissenting viewpoints, or an advisor openly communicating uncertainty. Such behaviors provide tangible indicators of decision quality and create opportunities for continuous improvement before the next consequential decision is made.

Consider a pension committee deciding whether to retain an underperforming investment manager. Traditional best practices provide a necessary foundation: review performance, evaluate fees, examine the mandate, and document the decision. An Augmented Intelligence approach can deepen that review by asking what evidence would justify retention, whether loyalty to the manager is influencing the discussion, and which alternative explanations remain untested.

A Special Purpose Avatar™ can support that examination through structured questioning. It can prompt participants to explain assumptions, identify missing information, and consider how they would respond if conditions deteriorate. It can present alternative viewpoints before consensus hardens.

Used appropriately, these capabilities strengthen deliberation, though their effectiveness depends upon reliable information, thoughtful design, and a willingness to challenge both individual and institutional assumptions.

The same partnership can also transform professional development. Traditional education delivers information at scheduled intervals. An intelligent avatar can provide continuous reinforcement when professionals encounter real-world dilemmas. It can adapt questions to demonstrated knowledge gaps, introduce progressively more difficult scenarios, and encourage reflection on actual decisions. This creates a path from understanding a principle to applying it under uncertainty and evaluating whether behavior is aligned with professional responsibilities.

None of this makes an avatar infallible. Generative AI can produce inaccurate statements, miss important context, and reinforce existing biases. Responsible augmentation therefore requires curated information sources, verification of consequential claims, clearly defined limitations, and ongoing human oversight. Fiduciaries remain accountable for accepting or rejecting the system’s recommendations.

The relevant question is not whether Artificial Intelligence is superior to human judgment. It is whether a disciplined partnership between technology and professional judgment produces better decisions than either can achieve independently.

The professional standard toward which the industry should move combines fiduciary judgment, AI proficiency, and Behavioral Governance. Professionals need sufficient technical understanding to question the system, sufficient ethical discipline to resist convenient answers, and sufficient leadership to act when evidence challenges consensus. Organizations should evaluate whether this combination improves the quality of inquiry, the treatment of uncertainty, and follow-through after decisions are made.

Traditional fiduciary best practices established an important foundation for prudent stewardship. Augmented Intelligence creates an opportunity to build beyond that foundation. Its value lies in making judgment more deliberate, behavior more observable, and accountability more continuous.

The most effective fiduciaries of the future will not merely demonstrate that they followed a prudent process. They will be able to demonstrate why their decisions deserve confidence. The next chapter of fiduciary excellence should reflect the best capabilities available today.

Don Trone is the CEO and Co-founder of the Behavioral Governance Institute which builds Special Purpose Avatars™ based on a 72 Cell | 288 Signal Meta-Framework. He was the principal founder of fi360 and is referred to as the ‘Father of Fiduciary.’
